title: Cross River Rail Authority reveals 'Esky Lid' flood barrier at Albert Street Station
text:
Cross River Rail Authority reveals 'Esky Lid' flood barrier at Albert Street Station
In short:
Engineers have unveiled an 80-tonne flood barrier at Albert Street Station.
The Cross River Rail Authority has dubbed the contraption "The Esky Lid".
What's next?
Cross River Rail is due to open in 2029, after repeated blowouts.
Engineers have completed an 80-tonne mechanical contraption named "The Esky Lid" designed to protect Brisbane's new underground tunnels from flooding.
The Esky Lid was unveiled today at Albert Street Station, which will be part of Brisbane's Cross River Rail underground train network.
Loading...
The 22-metre by 10-metre barrier will be able to descend from the ceiling over the station's main entrance, sealing it shut from floodwaters.
Sliding panels allow the barrier's modules to click into place, blending in with the station ceiling when not in use.
During intense flooding, shutters will also close off the entrance to the northern side of Albert Street Station.
Albert Street Station will be the most important line of defence, since it will be the deepest point of the 10-kilometre Cross River Rail network.
The station itself is in a low-lying, flood-prone area of Brisbane's CBD.
The lid will keep the station flood-proof up to about 10.3 metres above street level, which is rated as a 1-in-10,000-year probability.
Cross River Rail Delivery Authority program director Jeremy Kruger said they called it The Esky Lid because it could close like the lid of an esky.
Mr Kruger said passengers would be evacuated before the esky lid came down in the event of an extreme flood.
However, Mr Kruger said there was a good chance that people alive today would never see this "ingenious" feat of engineering in action.
"This will be a nice, open amenity 99.999 per cent of the time," Mr Kruger said.
"For that 0.001 per cent flood, it can come down, seal, deploy, and protect the station."
A history of blowouts
Mr Kruger said construction work would finish in early 2027, with safety tests to follow afterwards.
However, he said passenger services were not due to begin until 2029.
Cross River Rail was originally due to open in 2024 at a budget of $5.4 billion, but the project has suffered repeated blowouts over the years.
Mr Kruger said the project was now expected to cost around $19 billion, almost four times the original estimate.
It will be Queensland's single largest and most expensive infrastructure project in history.

title: Another Australian found safe after Nepal-Tibet flood disaster
text:
Another Australian found safe after Nepal-Tibet flood disaster
In short:
An eighth Australian has been found after the Nepal-Tibet flood.
The ABC understands that the person was not in the disaster zone.
Thirty-five other Australians remain unaccounted-for following the disaster.
Another Australian who had been unaccounted-for following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet has been found safe.
The ABC understands that the person was not in the disaster zone.
The person is the eighth Australian to be found since the floods, with 35 others still unaccounted-for.
Of those, 34 were on the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage, while one was not part of the tour.
For many Australian families, a relatively small area of mountainous terrain near the Nepal-Tibet border has become critical in the search for survivors, or at least answers.
Most Australians still unaccounted-for went missing near the Gyirong border crossing, north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, or in nearby areas inaccessible following the disaster.
Many were on spiritual pilgrimages to Mount Kailash, a mountain in south-western Tibet that Hindus consider sacred.
Rescue efforts continue at hydropower sites
In Nepal, rescue teams are continuing to focus on hydropower tunnel projects where some 900 people are missing.
Nepal's army said on Tuesday that 121 people could be trapped inside the tunnel network, with the remainder working elsewhere on the sites.
Nepal's disaster authority chief Dharma Raj Upreti told Reuters they were still focusing on finding survivors.
"Our bigger focus is on the Chilime hydroelectric project, where we believe people are trapped, because there was a canteen, residency and arrangements for food," he said.
He said teams were also focused on tunnels of the Upper Trishuli 3A and 3B projects, which were linked by an interconnected tunnel, where oxygen had been supplied by pipes and further equipment had been sent to build a passage to trapped workers.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said rescue operations would not stop.
"We know our responsibility and its sensitivity. We are translating the humanitarian spirit of the Nepali people into practice through the search and rescue operation," he said in a social media post late on Monday.
At least 1,399 people have been killed and more than 5,400 are still missing in Nepal and Tibet.
Chinese state media reported on Tuesday that none of the bodies recovered in Tibet were foreign nationals.
A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing, Chinese officials said, as they worked to identify the victims.
At least 43 people were killed in Tibet, with another 519 people still missing.
China's foreign ministry announced on Tuesday that a fourth batch of emergency aid had been sent to Nepal to help with rescue efforts.

title: Search for 900 missing hydro-plant workers continues in Nepal
text:
In short :
More than 100 hydropower workers are feared trapped in tunnels almost two weeks after floods ripped through the Himalayan site.
A total of 900 people are still missing from the hydro-electric tunnels in Nepal.
What's next?
Rescuers are working with specialised equipment to free people they believe may have air pockets inside the vast tunnel systems.
Nepali rescuers have searched for more than 100 hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels days after four miracle rescues from the wreckage of catastrophic floods that laid waste to towns and villages on the Himalayan border with China.
The rescues on Monday offered a glimmer of hope as Nepal marked the 13th day after the disaster, traditionally the final day of mourning in Hindu rites, for the hundreds killed in the floods.
About 121 of a total 900 people missing from the hydro-electric projects could have been trapped in these tunnels, army rescuers said.
Others may have been working elsewhere at the power plants but not inside the vast network of tunnels.
Among those rescuers were trying to find on Monday were four out of six people missing at the Chilime hydropower project in the hard-hit Rasuwa district who could still be alive, Shri Ram Neupane, a member of parliament involved in rescue efforts, told Reuters.
Authorities had obtained specialised equipment and identified techniques needed for the Chilime operation, Mr Neupane said.
Rescuers believe that there could be survivors trapped inside tunnels because many had air pockets, as well as spaces and rooms for people to stay, they said last week.
In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel on Saturday.
The others were two hydropower workers rescued from another tunnel on Friday and a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.
Government offices in the Hindu majority country and at missions abroad would fly the national flag at half-mast to mark the 13th day after death, the home ministry said in a statement.
The day is considered the final day of mourning by the faithful, who commemorate it with rituals and food offerings.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement last week, the Australian government would deploy a team of specialist drone operators to contribute to Nepal's search-and-rescue efforts.
"The team, including members of Fire and Rescue New South Wales and the Queensland Fire Department, will depart in the coming days as part of a 15-person Disaster Assistance Response Team," the statement read.
"They will use advanced drone technology to provide rapid mapping and imaging to support Nepali authorities' search operations."
At least 1,380 people have been killed by the mudslide. More than 5,500 are missing in Nepal and Tibet, among them 35 Australians.
The disaster was triggered on August 26 when a huge mass of mud and rock, following the collapse of part of a glacier, crashed into a river along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet region.
The resulting floods washed away towns and villages and buried roads and highways under mud and debris.
Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing in Tibet.
"The Chinese side will continue to make every effort to conduct search-and-rescue operations and handle post-disaster matters," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing.
China has faced pressure from some families of foreign visitors missing in Tibet, who say they have struggled to obtain information on missing relatives.
Mr Mao said Beijing would promptly release "updated information on the disaster situation and rescue activities."
On Sunday, China for the first time invited journalists from eight foreign media outlets, including Reuters, to visit the core affected areas.
With search teams still looking for survivors, Nepal's government has not planned any wider events for the final day of mourning.
"There are no government programs organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas," Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told Reuters.
President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, was touring flood-hit areas on Monday and would survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.
Security personnel at the district jail in Nuwakot, one of the two worst-affected districts, saved 923 prisoners by shifting them to a building in a higher location before floodwater entered their low-lying building on August 26, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post.
Authorities also captured 50 prisoners who had broken the prison wall and gates as flooding began, and had fled barely 100 metres, Shah said on Monday.
Reuters

title: Rescuers in Nepal pull two people alive from the debris 10 days after devastating floods
text:
Rescuers in Nepal pull two people alive from the debris 10 days after devastating floods
In short:
Rescuers in Nepal have pulled a Chinese national from a hydropower tunnel as efforts to save an estimated 900 people from the tunnel continue.
In a separate event, a woman was rescued from a damaged house in Nuwakot, Nepal.
What's next?
More than 5,000 people remain missing after the flood hit the Nepal-Tibet region on August 26.
Rescuers in Nepal have rescued two more survivors, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country.
The man and woman were freed in separate operations on Saturday, local time, with teams continuing the search for thousands of missing people.
A Chinese man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project.
Two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.
Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepali military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment.
Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.
A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man, called Lu Haitao, out of the tunnel.
CCTV shared audio of Mr Lu talking to an officer, saying how he repeatedly shouted whenever he saw the rescue crews' lights, but they could not hear him.
"When they rescued me today, when they shone [the light] before my eyes, I couldn't believe it,"
Mr Lu was taken to a hospital and was in stable condition, according to CCTV.
Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.
Woman's rescue 'has given hope to the entire nation'
In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman named Chandika Kumari Shrestha was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday.
Officials said she was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Ms Shrestha's rescue "has given hope to the entire nation".
Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud inside the damaged house.
They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a grey blanket.
At least 1,300 people were killed in the August 26 floods — which were likely caused by a glacier collapse — and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.
The United Nations has warned that the "magnitude of the destruction" makes delivering aid an immense challenge, as it launched a $US50 million ($69 million) appeal to help more than 84,000 people affected by the disaster.
On Saturday, the Nepali government released a provisional damage assessment, saying more than 7,500 houses, 48 public buildings and about 100 bridges had been destroyed.
With morgues overflowing, about 1,030 bodies have been buried in mass graves after having DNA samples taken for future identification, Nepal Police said on Saturday.
In a sign of progress, a team was able to reach the remote Nepal-China international border crossing at Timure in Rasuwa district on Saturday.
They placed Nepal's flag at the location, the prime minister said.
"After three days of continuous efforts, Nepal's national flag has been reinstalled along the Nepali border," he said on Facebook.
"It was extremely difficult to identify the border from the Nepali side and erect the flag."
AP/AFP

title: Nepali engineer working by river relives 'miracle' survival from deadly flash flood
text:
Nepali engineer working by river relives 'miracle' survival from deadly flash flood
In short:
Nepali engineer Rabindra Hamal was working by the river in the Rasuwa region when his colleagues radioed his team to run.
Mr Hamal recalled being 700 metres from base camp as a "large muddy wave" followed behind.
Two of his colleagues were swept away in the floods, while the surviving group of five were rescued four hours later.
Nepali engineer Rabindra Hamal has recalled the terrifying moments he and his colleagues outran an oncoming torrent of water and mud to clamber to safety.
Mr Hamal had been stationed at the hydropower plant by the Upper Trishuli river in Nepal's Rasuwa region on August 26 when colleagues working upstream sent them a dire warning.
The 46-year-old told the ABC that about 8:30am a colleague on the dam side of the river, about 10 kilometres upstream, relayed a message over the radio informing his team that disaster was heading their way.
"He was also running and was just saying, 'Please run, please run away, please run away, [a] huge flood is coming',"
"We immediately informed all our colleagues who were working with us in our office and rushed outside.
"Once we got outside, there was lots of confusion and panic around us."
A video shared among his colleagues shows the moment a large wave engulfed the dam as workers fled for their lives, closer to the Tibet border.
Loading...
Mr Hamal said himself and six others jumped in a vehicle and quickly started driving downstream to get as far away as possible.
He said they had only travelled 700 metres from their camp before they noticed a "large muddy wave" right behind them.
"It just looked like [something from a] Hollywood movie … I cannot even describe [it]," he said.
"We abandoned the vehicle … and started running towards higher ground.
"Fortunately, it was not the main flood wave because that gave [some of ] us enough time to reach … safe ground.
"But unfortunately, we lost our two friends."
He said the flood wave hit them but because of a small boulder in front of them, they were able to avoid the full impact of the wave and travel just five metres more to escape danger.
The engineer said two from his group of seven, a driver and cook, were not as lucky and were swept away in the flood waters before they could reach higher ground.
A verified video circulating online shows the base camp with red coloured rooftops, where Mr Hamal said his team were stationed, being destroyed by the flash flood just minutes after they escaped.
Ground began 'shaking violently' as second wave approached
Loading...
He said his group thought they were safe standing on a large boulder before the ground beneath their feet started "shaking violently" as a second, even larger flood wave approached.
"We were afraid that the rocks around us might fall … fortunately no rock fell and we were able to survive and stay their safely."
Four hours later, the surviving group of five heard a helicopter in the distance but they could not wave it down.
Mr Hamal said they spent the night covered in mud, on a boulder in the middle of the jungle.
"It was a very difficult and frightening night we experienced," he said.
"The next day, fortunately, we were rescued by helicopter, finally reached at home safely.
"It's completely miracle, I didn't believe that I could be able to survive, It's completely miracle."
Hundreds of hydropower workers remain missing
The group were eventually evacuated to a nearby army barracks before being evacuated to Kathmandu.
Geologist Harichandra Budhathoki was working at another hydropower site at the time, but by chance left just hours before the flood hit due to an unrelated medical emergency.
"The scale was so huge … no one could have imagined this," Mr Budhathoki said.
Both grateful to be alive, Mr Hamal and Mr Budhathoki decided to join the search effort and flew out to several work sites to look for survivors on Thursday.
"If we get [to save] one person's life, it will be very fruitful to my life, that's why Ineed to go there," Mr Hamal said while he waited for a helicopter to take him out to the Upper Trishuli 1 site.
Mr Budhathoki hoped his expertise could help find the dozens of workers who were believed to be trapped in hydro tunnels underground.
"I know every ins and outs of the tunnels, I know the alignment, the size, volume, so for the rescue team I should be able to provide the crucial details," Mr Budhathoki said.
Early on Friday, two people were rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, nine days after floods hit the area.
Nepali authorities have rescued about 300 people from hydropower projects in the region so far.

title: Mountainous area near Nepal-Tibet border becomes critical search zone for Australians
text:
Mountainous area near Nepal-Tibet border becomes critical search zone for Australians
Desperate Australians are flying to Nepal to search for their loved ones, still missing in the disaster.
Bhavin Patel films out the window of a helicopter while a navigation voice counts down the distance to its programmed destination: the last known coordinates of his wife, Reshma Patel.
No-one has heard from the 46-year-old Australian mother in the 11 days since a wall of water carved a path of destruction through Nepal and Tibet.
Her last known location was near the "Friendship Bridge" at the border — a crucial link between countries which has now been destroyed.
But Mr Patel is still hopeful his wife can be found alive.
He said hiring the helicopter was "not only for himself" but "for everyone [whose] family is lost over there".
Loading...
For many Australian families, a relatively small area of mountainous terrain near the Nepal-Tibet border has become critical in the search for survivors, or at least answers.
Most of those still unaccounted for went missing near the Gyirong border crossing north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu, or in nearby areas the disaster has left almost entirely cut off.
While seven missing Australians were found safe this week, the search for the 36 whose whereabouts remain unknown has grown increasingly desperate.
Kilometres of roads have been destroyed and dozens of bridges swept away, leaving helicopters as the main lifeline into some of the worst-affected communities.
Roads have been absorbed by riverbeds. Homes have been reduced to shells. Vehicles sit half-buried in mud.
And the destruction doesn't end at one village or one landslide. It runs for kilometres through the valley.
The search for survivors has taken to the skies, with helicopters and drones being brought in to canvass these crucial areas.
But some Australians say the official search efforts aren't going far enough and, despite the dire situation, believe their loved ones could still be out there.
A desperate search
Mr Patel landed in Kathmandu at 10pm last Friday night, with bloodshot eyes, anxious to gather any information he could about his wife and the search efforts in the disaster area.
The catastrophic flash flooding had torn through the region just two days before. The death toll has since climbed to more than 1,300, with another 5,500 still missing.
Most of the missing Australians, including Mrs Patel, were on spiritual pilgrimages to Mount Kailash, a mountain in south-western Tibet that Hindus consider sacred.
The Isha Foundation said their group of 80 people, including 11 Australians, was returning from the mountain and crossing back from Tibet into Nepal when the disaster struck.
Another tour operator, the US-based Himalayan Glacier Adventures, said 15 Australians travelling with its group went missing south of the border. Ten of them were expected to be somewhere along the road between the border crossing and the mountain village Syabrubesi, while the other five were believed to be back at their hotel in a nearby village.
Six Australians were travelling with a third company — Kailash Journeys — which said they last had contact with the group in Timure, a town about a 25-minute walk from the Gyirong immigration checkpoint.
Mrs Patel had travelled from her home in New South Wales to Nepal to go on the pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation.
The day after arriving in Kathmandu, Mr Patel visited hospitals in Nepal's capital and scoured lists that were being pinned up naming the injured retrieved from the disaster zone.
He met with the Isha Foundation and the Australian Government representatives, but he was left feeling "so helpless".
"I just tried from everywhere, but I'm not getting any help from there," he told the ABC last Sunday, while visiting a temple with his brother to pray.
On Thursday, Mr Patel hired a helicopter.
He had Reshma's phone records showing where her mobile last connected and used that to guide the journey.
But he said he was left "disappoint[ed]" and "frustrated" after flying over the area.
"No-one be there, not any rescues going over there," he said.
'We're in too much pain'
Other Australian family members, such as Aarti Raval and Chitrak Sharma, have been searching for signs of their loved ones remotely.
Mrs Raval's husband Bhavin Kumar, and Mr Sharma's parents Krishna and Umesh, are among the missing.
They have been poring over maps, last-known vehicle locations and data from mobile phone towers, trying to piece together where exactly their loved ones may have been when the flood hit.
Bhavin Kumar was on the Kailash Journeys tour, and Krishna and Umesh were on the Himalayan Glaciers tour, at the time of the flood.
Mrs Raval and Mr Sharma are looking for clues in that crucial mountainous area between the border and Syabrubesi, a Nepali village many hikers and pilgrims pass through on their journeys.
But more than a week after the disaster, getting to that region remains difficult.
Loading...
Local officials in Syabrubesi told the ABC hundreds of Nepalis and foreigners are feared to have been swept away.
Helicopters are bringing in food and medicine, and carrying out the dead and human remains recovered from the debris.
Those remains are being taken to the town of Trishuli, where authorities are carrying out the painstaking process of identification, including DNA collection, before families can be told whether their loved ones have been found.
And the danger isn't over. One resident of Syabrubesi, Riksing Lama, told the ABC that each night his family leave their home and sleep at a school on higher ground, for fear of another flood.
"Of course I am scared," he said.
"We're in too much pain."
Rescue challenges in both China and Nepal
Even the helicopters have limits in the search operations in Nepal.
Weather can close in quickly in these mountains, and in some of the worst-hit areas there are few safe places left to land.
Australia has sent a 15-person team of disaster specialists to Nepal, who will use drones to provide mapping and thermal imaging to "support search and rescue operations in areas that are difficult or too dangerous for ground crews to access."
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the deployment was part of "Australia's ongoing offers of assistance to Nepal".
The Pasang Lhamu Highway, where some of the Australians may have travelled before the floods hit, has been severely damaged — but Mrs Ravel and Mr Sharma have repeatedly urged authorities not to give up searching it, believing their loved ones may have escaped the floodwaters by reaching higher ground.
On the Tibetan side of the border, where Chinese authorities have listed six Australians as missing, there are other challenges.
The Chinese government, which governs Tibet, has been accused of censoring information about the disaster and underreporting casualties.
Earlier in the week Chinese state media reported that the route to the area had been largely cleared, allowing machinery to enter the area for in-depth search and rescue operations.
But Mr Patel said he did not see any sign of these efforts on his helicopter journey.
He wants the Australian disaster specialists to search in Tibet, as well as Nepal.
"They should [fly the drones] on the China side as well," he said.
China so far hasn't requested or accepted any international assistance with its search operations.
China's Foreign Ministry told the ABC the country was "making every effort to search for and rescue missing persons from both China and abroad".
It said it had deployed more than 2,300 rescue workers, 400 search-and-rescue vehicles, 8,000 pieces of search-and-rescue equipment and 800 drone flights.
"China is also maintaining close communication with foreign embassies in China and will continue to identify missing foreign nationals and handle follow-up matters," it said.
In an earlier statement, the Australian government said its officials in Beijing and Canberra were "engaging with Chinese authorities".
"We have consistently sought further and updated information on what the Chinese authorities know of any Australians involved in this tragedy and will continue to do so," it said.
Mr Patel has been told his wife is one of the six Australians listed as missing in Tibet.
The helicopter Mr Patel took to the region could not land there, so he is now investigating other options to reach the area, so he and his brother can search for his wife themselves.
Mr Patel is desperate to bring his wife home to their two children, who are waiting in Australia.
And despite planning to go it alone, he is still begging Chinese and Nepali teams to do more.
"There is still a chance we can save more life, and people are still waiting for you," he said.

title: Two people rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods, official says
text:
Two people rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods, official says
In short:
Two people have been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after devastating floods hit the country.
Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor, have been taken to hospital in Kathmandu, Reuters reported.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, local authorities say.
The office of Nepal's energy minister says two people have been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after floods hit the area.
Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha's office said in a statement that the two workers pulled from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station are Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor.
Loading...
Videos and photos released by Nepali authorities showed Mr Maharjan being pulled out of a hole in the ground amid cheering bystanders and put on a stretcher.
The other man, Mr Sah, was carried out on the back of a worker to a rescue tent, his face covered in mud.
In one of the videos, a team of army doctors attended to Mr Sah at a tent near the tunnel before he was taken to hospital, fitting what appeared to be an oxygen mask around his mouth and checking his vitals.
Mr Maharjan cannot move his hands and legs, but Mr Sah's injuries are not critical, an aide to the energy minister told Reuters news agency.
The two are being taken to an army hospital in Kathmandu, he said.
"I was humming the Hare Krishna Maha mantra inside,"
Both survivors are in the intensive care unit, a source from the army hospital where they were taken told Reuters, with their vital signs stable.
The 30-year-old said there were 35 to 45 people in the control centre when the floods hit.
"My responsibility in the control room was to save everybody's lives," he told a journalist shortly after his rescue.
"I told everybody about the situation and asked them to leave the room. In the process, I helped everybody get out, but I didn't have enough time to get out myself and run."
He said he believed there could still be some workers stuck inside the tunnel.
Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, said he has not received any news officially but has been told to go to the hospital.
"I have been hearing from the news that my brother has been found. The entire family is very happy,"
Roshani Maharjan, Kabir's sister-in-law, arrived at the army hospital with her sister — Mr Maharjan's wife — and told the ABC she always had faith he would be found.
"I am happy, deep in heart … We all believed that he would return back," she said.
"I am going to hug him."
Nepali politician Shri Ram Neupane posted news of the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue during the operation.
A team of experts in a WhatsApp group was guiding rescue workers in the search at the hydropower projects in what has become a valuable tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the race to find survivors.
More search and rescue operations were underway around the Upper Trishuli 3A project, the Nepali Army said.
Rescue efforts were being led by the army and police, with assistance from experts from India, South Korea and China.
Dhan Bahadur Tamang, who earlier escaped from a tunnel linked to the Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project, upriver from where the two men were pulled out on Friday, said their rescue was a miracle and raised the hope of finding more survivors.
Australian tunnelling expert helped rescue efforts from Melbourne
Melbourne geologist, Professor Arnold Dix, worked with authorities in Nepal from his home in the rural town of Monbulk as they scoured the devastated landscape looking for survivors.
Mr Dix told Charlie Pickering on 774 ABC Melbourne on Friday he was elated to receive news of the latest rescues.
"We're decent human beings and our calculations and analysis said, there could be people alive in there, conditions might have allowed life to continue," he said.
"And we have — we got two. And more to come, I hope."
Mr Dix said the Australian government asked him to fly to Nepal in the aftermath of the disaster, but he stayed in Monbulk because he had a solid data connection there that allowed him to connect with rescuers on the ground.
"That meant helping the team identify where the power station used to be, using satellite images coming out of helicopters," he told ABC News Channel.
"And then comparing that with the engineering drawings … Then we figured out where we were going to drill.
"We've done something that we've never done, ever, in the history of the world."
Mr Dix said the use of explosives to blow up damaged land and infrastructure to remove it in the hope of finding tunnel entry-ways has never been done before.
"This is extraordinary," he said.
"For me, it means all those all-nighters that we've been doing to try and pull this off have been worth it."
Mr Dix said the two survivors were located about 60 metres into the entrance of an underground tunnel and workers at the site are continuing to drill to unearth another 150 metres leading to the rest of the power station.
"If we've got live people there, we're hopeful that we're going to get some more good news," he said.
Mr Dix said he is now travelling to Nepal to join the rest of the team he had been working with from afar.
The rescues come nine days after the August 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, that devastated towns and valleys in Nepal.
At least 1,287 people were killed and 5,083 still missing, according to the latest figures released by the country's disaster management agency on Friday.
China, as of late Friday, said 31 people were killed and 531 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.
About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.
Thirty-six Australians remain unaccounted-for in the areas affected by the floods, while Australian disaster response specialists left for Nepal on Friday to join the search for survivors.
Property, housing and infrastructure worth at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($3.57 billion) were lost in the flooding catastrophe, according to Dharma Raj Upreti, the chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Nepal will need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, Mr Upreti said on Thursday, with at least 7,500 of those homes destroyed.

title: Bundaberg restaurateurs describe running up mountain to escape wall of water in Nepal
text:
A Queensland couple has described their escape after being caught in the inland tsunami in Nepal.
The couple, who were on a holiday visiting family, ran up a mountain with their three-year-old daughter to escape floodwaters.
What's next:
They are still searching for other family members, but fear none have survived.
A Queensland couple has told of their traumatic escape after being caught in the inland tsunami in Nepal, where they were on a family holiday.
Pramila Dangol and Clinton Baker, from Bundaberg, were visiting family with their three-year-old daughter when a collapsed glacier caused catastrophic flooding in Betrawati on August 26.
They said the village was given 15 minutes' warning before the wall of water struck.
"When it hit the buildings, it just blew up," Mr Baker said.
"It was pretty traumatic for me, and us, and everyone else."
The family ran up a mountain, Mr Baker carrying his daughter, Prammisha, to safety.
"He was strong and ran quick," Ms Dangol said.
"I couldn't believe it," Mr Baker said.
"At the time, you heard the sound, the rumbling through the ground."
From the mountain, they watched as the buildings and people below them were swallowed by the wave of water and debris.
People could be seen in the distance clambering onto the rooftops of buildings "three and four storeys" high.
"The waves are higher than the building itself," Mr Baker said.
Ms Dangol's family home, where she was born and grew up, was washed away.
"Nothing left, yeah," she said through tears.
"In that house, I had Mum, Dad, you know, the memories, a lot of our childhood photos, everything."
More than a week after the disaster, they are still searching for many of her extended family.
"I've been posting on Facebook every day," Ms Dangol said.
"We know that no-one [is] alive, but at least we can find the dead bodies."
The couple, who own a restaurant in Bundaberg, had travelled to Nepal for family ceremonies and it was the first time they had taken their daughter to the country.
"I wanted her [Prammisha] to [see] where I spent [my] childhood," Ms Dangol said.
"I used to go to the river for swimming when I was [in] primary and my high school time. That was a very good time there."
Mr Baker said he was "still shaken up" and was anxious to get back to Australia, but trying to remain positive.
"Just don't take life for granted," he said.
"I'm just trying to stay strong … can't wait to get home."

title: Nepali photographer battles emotional toll while documenting flood devastation
text:
Nepali photographer battles emotional toll while documenting flood devastation
Desperate families crowd around a small army centre in Nuwakot, Nepal, tracing their fingers through hundreds of names taped up on a wall, hoping to find their loved ones listed as survivors.
Nepali photographer and documentary filmmaker Rasik Maharjan was there to film it, witnessing their "hands trembling" as they scoured the lists waiting for good news.
Rasik told the ABC that people have been waiting by the helipads day and night for the army and rescue teams to arrive.
"Every time a helicopter approaches, everyone looks up. There is a quiet hope that the next person coming through the door might be someone they have been waiting for," he said.
"It is an exhausting kind of waiting."
Names and photos of the missing are pasted on public buildings in disaster zones. (Supplied: Rasik Maharjan)
Family members of the missing have been desperately checking lists of survivors. (Supplied: Rasik Maharjan)
The list of survivors has been growing as search efforts continue. (Supplied: Rasik Maharjan)
Families have been waiting day and night by helipads for rescue teams to arrive. (Supplied: Rasik Maharjan)
The weight of the tragedy first hit Rasik when he couldn't find the name of one of his missing school friends on the lists.
Knowing someone who was caught up in the wreckage on a personal level "changes everything", he said.
"It stops being just a story you are covering and turns into an agonising, personal nightmare every time I look at the boards or the faces around the camp."
Whole villages wiped out 'terrifying' to witness
Originally based in Kathmandu, Rasik travelled 60 kilometres west to Nuwakot to document the Nepal-Tibet flood devastation.
Nuwakot is a town located on the bank of the Trishuli and Tadi Rivers, where bordering villages have been devastated by catastrophic flash flooding.
He remembered when he first heard about the flooding while sipping his morning coffee on August 26, thinking it would be like previous disasters he'd covered.
But as he started watching videos of "whole villages wiped out and seeing so many people missing", he said he realised how bad things were getting, and he and his friend got on their scooters and travelled towards the devastation.
"It didn't fully hit me until we were on the road," he said.
"It looked terrifying."
Loading...
High-resolution satellite imagery has shown structures and settlements wiped off the map as glacial waters ripped through neighbourhoods.
The Nepal-Tibet floods have killed at least 1,252 people and thousands are still missing, including 38 Australians
In some of the hardest hit areas, bodies of those killed by a devastating flood have been found more than 100 kilometres downstream.
'The camera became a kind of shield'
When Rasik arrived, he said the atmosphere in Nuwakot was "heavy" with a combination of despair and "a quiet, suffocating tension".
Being behind the camera and watching people lose their homes, belongings and loved ones made "the camera become a kind of shield".
By the sixth day in Nuwakot, the emotional toll he said he often pushed aside in order to keep documenting difficult moments started to seep through.
"Something inside me just broke,"
"I was standing there watching the water rise. I wanted to cry. I wanted to let everything out.
"But I couldn't.
"Not here. Not while people were still waiting for their loved ones."
As a photographer and documentary maker, he said it had been difficult to process what had happened to his country while still continuing to do his job effectively.
"People see the final photograph or video on their screens. They don't see the silence inside the vehicle on the long drive back," he said.
"They don't see how heavy the equipment feels after days in the field. And sometimes, you don't want to hold a camera anymore.
"You just want to put it down and use your hands to help carry someone to safety."
Documenting survival 'never just a job'
Over the past week, Rasik has heard extraordinary stories of survival.
A group of school children told him they had been swept away by floodwater and miraculously survived by scrambling to the banks just in time to run to safety.
That was one of several stories that had stuck with him already, and he's eager to capture more.
Rasik said being behind the camera to capture this devastating event was his way of helping, by showing people what's happening on the ground.
But at times, it hasn't been easy.
"There are moments when I ask myself: 'Why am I even doing this? Do I really need to capture this? Does the world really need to see this moment?' But then I remind myself why I am here," he said.
"This is what I can do.
"I may not be able to rescue someone or change what has already happened, but I can document it, make sure their story is seen.
"Documenting survival and sorrow is never just a job."

title: Nepal's peak trekking season is approaching but its guides are in mourning
text:
Nepal's peak trekking season is approaching but its guides are in mourning
At this time of year, trekking guide Eka Devi Mainali would normally be going about her usual preparations for Nepal's peak season.
But instead she's waiting to hear if her friends' bodies have been found, 19 of them.
"I have lost many friends and people I personally knew in this devastating disaster," Ms Mainali told the ABC.
Nepal's peak hiking season runs from September to November.
But for many guides like Ms Mainali, who lead foreigners through the Himalayas each year, they must now carry something heavier into the mountains, their grief.
"It feels very difficult to talk about tourism or business without first thinking about the human tragedy," she said.
"This is not simply a natural disaster. It is a deeply painful time for families who have lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods."
Ms Mainali founded her own trekking company, SheGuide Treks, and has guided tourists along Nepal's most popular routes, including Everest Base Camp, for more than a decade.
Each year, she dedicates 10 per cent of her company's profits towards supporting and empowering women and children.
"My intention is bigger than myself. I want to build something that creates opportunities for women and allows me to give back to children and communities as well," she said.
Speaking from her office in Kathmandu, Ms Mainali sorts through piles of children's clothing she has collected to donate to those in areas affected by the floods.
She described the process as "incredibly painful".
She has taken responsibility for coordinating with the families of her 19 friends who are still missing.
"I am standing with their wives and children, doing my best to support and represent their families during this difficult time," she said.
Nepal said 1,118 bodies had so far been recovered, while more than 3,900 people remained missing. At least 38 Australians are among those unaccounted-for.
Conflicted between pain and livelihood
For guides like Shishir Sapkota, the flood spared his own family and friends.
But in a trekking community as tight-knit as Nepal's, this type of loss is felt beyond bloodlines.
"As guides, we are connected to many people in the trekking and local communities, so when something like this happens, it affects us all emotionally, even if our own families are safe," he told the ABC.
Mr Sapkota has been running his tour business, Mato Manchey Ra Himal, for three years.
He said he enjoyed working as a guide because trekking was "not only about reaching a destination".
"It is also about experiencing the local culture, meeting people and sharing the beauty of Nepal with visitors," he said.
Thinking of the people who have lost their lives, homes and livelihoods, Mr Sapkota said he was toeing the line between sadness and worry about the upcoming trekking season.
"Tourism is the livelihood of many guides, porters, hotel owners, transport workers and local communities,"
Mr Sapkota said he had tours booked for this season, but the current situation had made his plans uncertain.
He said he hoped for the best for the affected areas and also hoped the trekking season could continue safely.
"Nepal and the people working in tourism need the support of visitors now more than ever."
Trip to Nepal 'not only a holiday'
Tourism operators are keeping tours running while assessing damage to roads and communities.
Intrepid Travel, which operates 26 tours in Nepal, said its customers and staff were safe and it was supporting affected local partners and host families.
"We are closely monitoring developments and continuing to assess the impact on current trips, transportation and accommodation," said Yalamber Rai, Intrepid's general manager for Nepal.
Two of its itineraries pass through the affected region, including the Tamang Heritage and Langtang Valley Trek.
Both normally include an overnight stay in Syabrubesi, a village that suffered significant damage.
"These floods will have lasting impacts on livelihoods, trade, tourism and local businesses," Mr Rai told the ABC.
Tourism is a vital part of the country's economy, with data showing it made up close to 7 per cent of GDP pre-pandemic.
Nepal's tourism minister, Khadak Raj Paudel, this week urged travellers not to cancel their trips.
"Your coming to Nepal this time does not mean only a holiday. It's a big support to the country fighting this catastrophic tragedy," he said.
Operators also had a clear message: Nepal's industry has not stopped, but routes must be carefully monitored.
"We believe it is important that travel continues responsibly in the regions that are stable and therefore operational," said Sue Badyari, the CEO of World Expeditions, a tour company operating for more than 50 years in Nepal.
'Strength and solidarity' on display
Kathmandu's airport remains fully functional, and Nepal's major trekking regions including Annapurna, Everest and Kanchenjunga are operating as normal.
"For people feeling anxious, our message is that Nepal is a large and geographically diverse country," Ms Badyari said.
"The devastation in the affected communities is immense, but it does not mean the whole country or all trekking regions have been impacted.
"One of the best ways to support Nepal right now is by continuing with planned treks."
He stressed the resilient nature of Nepalis who depend on tourism.
"They live alongside the mountains and know their power, and they are, sadly, no strangers to natural disaster. That doesn't make a loss like this any easier," Ms Badyari said.
"They are deeply saddened by the events of last Wednesday, as anyone would be, but there is a strength and a solidarity in these communities that continues to move us.
"We are humbled by the quiet courage they continue to show."
For travellers already in the region, the challenge is more immediate.
Utsav Aryal, director of the Nepalese Australian Welfare Society, said those stranded at places like Gosaikunda Lake were being urged to use different paths.
"While an easterly route is an option, it is much longer and far more treacherous for older people to hike compared to the usual western route," he said.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's Smartraveller website has advised those going to Nepal to "reconsider" travelling to the flood-affected areas of the Bhote-Koshi and Trishuli rivers due to the risk of landslides and further flooding.
"There remains a high risk of further flooding, landslides and debris flows in affected areas," it said.

title: Australians travel to Nepal to search for missing relatives
text:
Australians travel to Nepal to search for missing relatives
In short:
Relatives of Australians who have been missing since the catastrophic floods have flown to Nepal to look for answers.
Several families have raised concerns about the official search for survivors, particularly during the crucial first days after the disaster.
Nepal's communication minister defended the government's response to the crisis, telling the ABC in an exclusive interview that the rescue mission was "not an easy job".
Jony Raval's phone does not stop ringing.
He has been in Kathmandu for just two hours, and already his family wants to know what he has found.
"I didn't come here to be a story," Jony says.
"I came here to fulfil a promise to my sister. That I won't leave here without her husband."
Jony has barely slept in a week.
His brother-in-law, Bhavinkumar Raval, is one of 38 Australians missing after catastrophic floods tore through the Nepal-Tibet border region.
Bhavinkumar had been heading to the sacred Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage with two close friends and fellow Australians, Karan Bhardwaj and Arpan Kothari.
Six days after the disaster, Jony left his home in Gujarat, India, and flew to Kathmandu to look for them himself.
Back in Brisbane, his sister, Aarti Raval, has spent almost every waking hour trying to work out where her husband was when the floods hit.
Australian family trawls the internet for clues
The mother-of-two has trawled photographs, videos and social media posts, searching for anything that might narrow down his last known location.
She tracked down a photograph of one of Bhavinkumar's fellow travellers, taken on the morning of the disaster. In it, the man is standing on a muddy road in a steep valley surrounded by lush green mountains.
Bhavinkumar was travelling with Kailash Journeys in a group of 26 foreign travellers, including six Australians and people from the United States, United Kingdom, New Zealand, Malaysia, Canada and South Africa. They were accompanied by five Nepali guides and staff.
Aarti points to a statement from the tour company saying its last contact with the group was at 7:30am in Timure on the morning of the disaster.
Timure is about a 25-minute walk from the Gyirong immigration checkpoint, which was struck by the flooding roughly an hour later.
From that information, Aarti believes she has narrowed down the stretch of road where her husband may have been.
She pulls up coordinates on Google Maps.
The location is along the Pasang Lhamu Highway, hemmed in by dense forest and steep cliffs.
"Bhavin is still somewhere in that mud area just above the immigration office and no rescue search has been going there," she says.
"All I want is someone to go through helicopter, drop some people inside the bush area and go and find those people who are stuck in the mud.
"I'm sure they are there and still breathing."
Every piece of information vital in search
For Aarti and other families, every fragment of information has become important.
They have spent the past week combing through videos from the disaster zone, survivor accounts, immigration records and lists of the missing and rescued, trying to reconstruct what happened.
Some of the material cannot be independently verified. But for families desperate for answers, even the smallest new detail can feel like a lifeline.
Aarti says she has passed her research to Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, but has been frustrated by the response.
"I'm not sure if they're even looking into my request because I am not feeling that I have been supported by them at all," she says.
"They have no answers whatsoever."
She has also sent the information to Nepal Police, but says she has seen little movement.
"I had to send my brother from India to Kathmandu, and he is now at least looking for him," she says.
"At least I have my own person, my own eyes on the ground who is genuinely looking for my husband."
That is now Jony's task.
Armed with the information his sister has gathered, he plans to go first to the Kailash Journeys office in central Kathmandu, then to Nepal's immigration authorities and the Chinese embassy.
His most basic question is also one the family has been unable to answer: which side of the border were the three men on when the floods hit?
Jony says the lack of information from China has made the search harder.
Many relatives travel to Nepal to find answers themselves
The Australian government said its officials in Beijing and Canberra were "engaging with Chinese authorities".
"We have consistently sought further and updated information on what the Chinese authorities know of any Australians involved in this tragedy, and will continue to do so," it said.
The ABC understands Bhavinkumar Raval, Karan Bhardwaj and Arpan Kothari are not among the six Australians identified as unaccounted-for on the Chinese side of the border.
Jony is not the only relative who has come to Kathmandu looking for answers.
In recent days, other family members of missing Australians have arrived, including the husbands of Reshma Patel and Sumi Adhikari and relatives of the Iyer family.
Bhavin Patel told the ABC he would not leave Nepal without finding his wife.
Sumi Adhikari's husband, Rava Pandey, said he had "accepted the reality of what has happened" and would start final rituals on Thursday.
Several families have raised concerns about the speed and scale of the search during the crucial first days after the disaster.
About 1.6 million people affected by the disaster
The Nepali government also faced criticism after initially declining general offers of international search-and-rescue teams.
In an interview with the ABC, Nepal's minister for communication and information technology, Dr Bikram Timilsina, defended the government's response.
"During this kind of disaster there are so many friendly countries which have supported us and which also expressed their intention of working in the rescue zones," he said.
"It is not an easy job to do, and it depends on the geography, the context, and so many cultural factors as well, so we needed to understand that the help would really be helpful."
He said assistance was accepted once authorities determined where international help could be most useful.
At the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority in Kathmandu, officials are now running the emergency response from a central situation room.
Teams are mapping destruction, monitoring road closures and trying to determine where rescue teams and aid should be sent.
According to the disaster authority, 1.6 million people have been affected and thousands remain cut off from food and essential services.
Officials say helicopters are carrying out regular reconnaissance flights around the border region, but the scale of the destruction has made landing in some areas impossible.
Kailash Journeys says it has also been searching for the missing group. The company conducted its own helicopter reconnaissance flight on the day of the floods, checked hospitals and medical facilities and has been monitoring official lists and images of those found.
Families cling to hope their loved ones will return
Aarti says the uncertainty has been especially hard on her two sons, aged 13 and eight.
"It was extremely hard to convince them what we are doing and why we are doing," she says.
"They are not wanting to lose hope that their daddy is coming home."
Neither is she.
Aarti says she wants Nepalese authorities to search every possible area around her husband's last known location.
"Send some troops inside those areas behind the immigration top hills and find those people."

title: Inside the mission to reach Nepal's underground 'Goldilocks zones'
text:
Inside the mission to reach Nepal's underground 'Goldilocks zones'
The tunnels were built to harness the power of Nepal's rushing mountain rivers. Now, they have become the focus of one of the country's most desperate rescue missions.
Scenes from the floods in Nepal and Tibet are catastrophic. But another disaster is unfolding underground and out of sight.
More than 900 workers linked to hydropower projects in flood-ravaged districts near the two countries' border are feared trapped after a cataclysmic deluge of ice, rock, mud and water swept through the region last Wednesday.
Under floodlights and a backdrop of collapsed hillsides, rescuers are excavating around the clock in a bid to reach those trapped underground.
Their condition remains unknown.
But Melbourne-based geologist and engineer Arnold Dix, who was invited by Nepalese authorities to provide advice on the rescues, says any survivors could live for as long as 17 days.
He says some of the underground power stations likely withstood the immense pressure of the flash flooding. However, it remains unclear whether emergency systems activated in time or whether water and debris inundated them.
Professor Dix describes the terrain as a "lunar landscape".
"Everything is just missing," he says, and that is making it difficult to even find the access tunnels for the underground power stations.
For rescuers, each site presents its own challenge.
This map shows the layout of the Trishuli 3B hydro power plant.
As water flows down the river, some is diverted into the plant's intake and through a kilometres-long "headrace tunnel" that runs under the mountains that tower immediately beside the riverbanks.
It then reaches the powerhouse, where the energy of the rushing water is converted into electricity.
"The deluge basically wiped out 27 power stations," Professor Dix says. "Of them, 12 are destroyed, and there's nothing left at the surface.
"We are focusing our efforts on the subterranean spaces that we know will have survived the impact of that debris coming down the valley."
Those efforts are focused on the power station structures themselves, not the 'headrace' tunnels that carry water through the systems.
The Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where Professor Dix is assisting, includes a 33-metre facility that is buried underneath the mountains.
Rooms inside these underground structures, along with supplies, such as water and equipment, could improve the chances of survival for any trapped workers, although dwindling air supplies remain a major concern.
Forty-two workers have been reported missing here, and rescuers are concentrating on locating and entering the access tunnel that leads to the underground powerhouse.
Photos taken during the construction phase of the plant provide a sense of its enormous scale.
The Trishuli River once flowed well below the entrance to this tunnel.
Now, the riverbed itself lies buried beneath flood debris and there's no visible sign of the tunnels at the surface.
"The topography completely changed," Professor Dix says.
"We had to use advanced satellites, technical drawings and vision coming in from the helicopters on the ground to find the exact right locations."
Search and rescue efforts have also been hampered by poor weather, mud, and the loss of critical infrastructure like roads and bridges.
Despite the uncertainty, there is hope some workers may have reached what engineers refer to as the "Goldilocks zone".
"The Goldilocks zone, where we think people might be, is right up at the top of the underground powerhouse in the area between where the tunnels enter the power station and the roof," Professor Dix says.
This cross-section diagram of the powerhouse shows what Professor Dix is talking about — if rescuers are to find any survivors, they are likely to be in the highest section of the 11-storey underground structure, above the power cubicle.
"So that's where we're hoping that people [are] who've survived the initial explosion — and that's effectively what this is. It's not a flood, it's an explosion.
"There's plenty of air there in the Goldilocks zone, and it's a large space. If there was any place you were going to survive, it would be there."
Jenjen Lama, a mountain guide involved in the search-and-rescue operations, says a similar operation is underway at the Chilime Hydropower Station and has provided the ABC with a diagram of where engineers believe survivors may be located.
The cross-section image shows a 250-metre tunnel leading downhill before connecting with the powerhouse, which includes a service bay, control room and the hydropower transformer.
Again, experts believe the area at the top of the underground powerhouse is where survivors could be located.
But reaching these areas presents its own challenges.
Professor Dix says it will likely require rescuers to drill vertically from the surface and then break through reinforced concrete at the top of the powerhouse.
He is working on a strategy to do exactly that.
However, one of the major concerns for rescuers is the fact that mud and water found at the tunnel entrance could indicate flooding deeper inside the facility.
"If the water's there, that probably means we've got water in the powerhouse up above the level we want," Professor Dix says.
A rescue beyond the textbook
Professor Dix has advised on major underground rescue operations around the world. Three years ago, he was hailed a Himalayan hero after helping rescue 41 workers who had been trapped for 17 days after a tunnel collapsed in India.
But he says the conditions in Nepal are unlike anything he has encountered.
"There are boulders bigger than houses — I've never seen that before in my life," Professor Dix says. "It's just an extraordinary operation."
Although helicopters are ferrying personnel and supplies into some of the hardest-hit areas, payload restrictions have constrained what equipment can be brought in.
In the early days, crews were restricted to machinery weighing less than three tonnes, Professor Dix said, forcing rescuers to rely largely on "hands and shovels" in what he described as an operation "well outside any textbook rescue".
Since then, access has improved and some larger machines have been brought into the area.
Filmmaker and drone pilot Manish Maharjan, who has been volunteering with the Nepalese army, says some tunnels are "filled with mud like toothpaste in a tube".
At one hydropower project, he used a drone to search to the end of a tunnel but found no sign of life.
But as long as there remains a chance that hydropower workers are alive in pockets of air underground, the search continues.
In a social media post, Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said 279 workers had been rescued so far.
Arnold Dix is an optimist, though he admits the situation is dire.
"If there are people alive out there, we are doing our best to find them."

title: The turquoise home that withstood the Nepal floods
text:
When the floodwaters tore through the town of Trishuli in the Nuwakot district in Nepal, most of the valley vanished in minutes.
Homes folded, bridges collapsed and the Trishuli river rose by up to nine metres in just 30 minutes.
But on the second floor of this turquoise home, a family of five stood watching the disaster swallow up their town.
What happened on the day?
On the morning the flood hit, the river rose with a speed that left residents little time to react.
Lakshmi Pandey said she was at their shop, about five minutes away from their home, when she realised the flood was coming.
"We ran back as fast as we could because my mother-in-law and my daughter were at home," she said in an interview with The Economic Times, translated by the ABC.
The mother of two told her mother-in-law, "The flood is coming, we need to run".
A surge triggered upstream saw a deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris carve a trail of destruction through the country's valley towns and villages.
Within minutes, streets were underwater.
"The old bridge broke and a huge amount of water suddenly came rushing down from above, and at that point, I realised that we could no longer escape by running outside,"
Inside the turquoise house close to the riverbank, the mother, her husband, daughter, in-laws and their neighbour remained trapped.
Her son was at school at the time.
They watched from their balcony, standing next to their washing machine, as the flood ripped through the bottom floor of their home.
In a viral video, the family can be seen huddling around the balcony rails in what's been dubbed the "miracle house" and "greenhouse" on social media.
"Water was hitting the house from both sides, and the whole house started shaking; it felt just like the huge shaking we experienced during the 2015 Nepal earthquake," she said.
Loading...
As the houses around them collapsed from the force of the flood, the couple described feeling like there was no chance that they would survive.
"I thought my son would be all alone now, an orphan," the mother said in a Reuters interview.
"We thought if we survive we will all survive, if we die we will all die."
Her husband, Prakash Pyakurel, recalled thinking "this is the end," deciding the family should stay together for what felt like their last moments while "chanting the God's name."
Waiting to be rescued, the mother said she told herself "we are five people, we should be patient".
Footage circulating on Saturday showed rescue workers using a makeshift bridge to reach the family, with mud seen stuck on the walls slightly below the balcony.
Loading...
The mother said four neighbours risked their own lives and came to rescue them.
"Somehow, they managed to get all of us out safely," she said.
Why is the turquoise house still standing?
The head of engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Adrian McCallum, said it was likely the water was able to flow underneath the house, similar to a traditional Queenslander, lessening loads upon the structure.
"Crucially, the turquoise house appears to be built on rock and constructed of concrete with reinforcing steel," he told the ABC.
The house appears to be protected from the main river flow by a small headland protruding immediately upstream, so this may also have saved it from the main brunt of the flood, he said.
The disaster is believed to have activated when part of a Himalayan glacier broke off and crashed into the river below and triggered flash flooding and a mudslide.
As of Tuesday, the death toll surpassed 1,000 as rescuers deployed heavy machinery, helicopters and excavators to reach thousands still missing for nearly a week.
Hundreds remain stranded at devastated hydropower stations and are the focus of rescue efforts.
Specialised rescue teams from China, India and Nepal have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dig through the ruins of hydropower projects, using excavators to try to rescue the nearly 300 workers trapped inside tunnels.
Family returns to 'miracle home'
On Monday, the surviving family walked back through their home — that remains standing — to assess the damage.
What had been their town just a few days earlier was now a field of mud.
The mother expressed gratitude that her family, including her son, had been "reborn".

title: Four Australians found safe in Nepal, but 38 others still missing
text:
Four Australians found safe in Nepal, but 38 others still missing
In short:
Four more Australians have been found safe after the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, but 38 others remain missing.
Families of those still missing are urging authorities to do more to find their loved ones.
At least 1,135 people have been killed and more than 4,000 others remain missing.
Four more Australians have been confirmed safe in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, but 38 others remain unaccounted-for as loved ones urge authorities to do more to find those missing.
Five Australian citizens have been located safe since Tuesday morning.
One person was found in Nepal and another in China, while three others were found outside the disaster zone.
The ABC understands those confirmed safe on Wednesday had not had contact with families or next of kin since the flood, and their welfare could not initially be confirmed.
Nepal said at least 1,114 people had died, while 3,916 people remained missing.
China's state media reported 21 dead and 541 missing, taking the overall number of reported dead to 1,135 and missing to more than 4,000.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far.
Rescuers are focusing on hydropower plant projects where hundreds of workers are believed to have been trapped.
Images released by Nepal's army show teams working through debris-filled tunnels to find signs of life.
Victorian resident Anamika Shrestha hopes her 65-year-old engineer father, Ganesh Mani Shrestha, is safe.
The Geelong mother of two said her father, who is not an Australian citizen, was working on a construction site at the Rasuwagadhi Integrated Customs Checkpoint on the Nepal-Tibet border.
She was frustrated it took rescue teams about six days to reach the area where her father had been and said more international help was needed.
"We need specialised missing person search teams and then forensic and DNA support, and proper identification of anyone who has been recovered," Ms Shrestha said.
Her family is hopeful her father is alive but is also desperate to find his body if he has died.
"If we don't get the body … it's going to be really difficult for us thinking that maybe his soul is still not resting in peace," she said.
"At this stage we don't need any sympathy or reassurance, we just need timely action."
Her brother in Nepal has submitted DNA to authorities in the hope her father's body will be found and identified, but she said it could take months.
"We are still hoping he's safe somewhere. Most of the people are saying if he was safe then we would have heard about it already. It's been eight days now," she said.
The Australian government is providing $8 million in support for Nepal, with emergency supplies including shelter, hygiene and solar light kits delivered by the Australian Defence Force on Wednesday.
Eighteen Australian response team personnel are also on the ground in Nepal to assist with the rescue efforts.
In China, rescue teams used search dogs to search rubble for people trapped at the Gyirong Port border crossing, which was completely destroyed.
Chinese state media reported on Wednesday that the road had been reopened and extra personnel were at the site to search for those missing.
Authorities have begun burying hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling, with mortuaries overflowing in Nepal.
At least 17 bodies have also been pulled from rivers downstream in India.

title: Six months after record flooding, Nauiyu remains damaged and without key services
text:
Six months after record flooding, Nauiyu remains damaged and without key services
At the end of a dust-laden road on the banks of the Daly River, the remote Indigenous community of Nauiyu bears the scars of disaster.
The entrance road is marred by large potholes eating into speed bumps, while mounds of silt line the outskirts of town.
It has been three months since residents of Nauiyu, also known as Daly River, returned home after back-to-back record floods in February and March forced them to evacuate.
Outside his house at the end of town, life-long Nauiyu resident James Parry can point to the exact step the floodwaters rose to.
"It covered 15 stairs — the whole bottom half of the house," he said.
"The tables were flipped over, the couches were flipped, my bed, my freezer."
He said he was one of the luckier members of the community, as he and his family were able to move some of their belongings upstairs.
"Everybody else lost everything — cars, homes, the lot," he said.
Mr Parry said the 2026 floods were the worst he has ever seen and there is mounting frustration that key services in the community were not yet fully online.
"The aged care centre is full of asbestos, and we only have a few old people left," he said.
"Kids are not turning up to school since they got back; the teachers have to go around door-to-door to get these kids to come to school."
He also said various repair works have not been done well, noting large gaps beneath doors leading to dust travelling inside and glass windows replaced with plastic.
"Some of those council homes had wooden benches, wooden drawers, wooden floors, they were all ripped out," he said.
Up until Tuesday, a boil water alert was still in place for the community, with pallets of bottled water packages routinely unloaded outside the Nauiyu general store.
Residents including Mr Parry said there was broad confusion over the water quality.
"No-one's told us anything,"
In a statement on Wednesday, NT Health said the boil water alert for Nauiyu had been lifted the day before and it had notified the community.
"It is safe for Naiuyu residents to use tap water for all purposes; however, bottled water should be used to make up baby formula for infants 12 months and under," a spokesperson said.
"Power and Water provides free bottled water for this purpose."
'It doesn't feel like home'
Nauiyu resident Kieren Karritpul said the damage had fundamentally changed the town.
"This place is not really 100 per cent," he said.
"It doesn't feel like home."
As of the end of August, several residential buildings in the community were still without power, impacting living arrangements and preventing key workers from returning to the community.
"My brother and my niece have been staying over at my house because their house still doesn't have power," Mr Karritpul said.
On a shady street in the centre of the community, Merrepen Arts Centre, where Mr Karritpul works, stands dormant among mounds of dirt and damaged art materials.
The centre, which employs more than 40 artists, is one of the buildings that has gone without power since the flood, depriving residents of a source of income and community.
"Every now and then I get pulled up at the shop or clinic by people asking when it will open, or when they will get their canvases," he said.
"We have to tell [tourists] to go on the three-hour drive to Darwin if they want to buy things."
Though empty and without power, Merrepen Arts Centre managers have still been issued a power and water bill covering "fixed daily charges" for the first half of 2026.
Questions raised around flood response
The sorry state of Nauiyu several months on from the floods has prompted questions about plans for remediation.
After the last wet season, the Northern Territory government announced a $100 million flood recovery fund to repair damaged infrastructure and aid with flood mitigation.
So far, only $12.5 million of the fund has been spent, with just $500,000 put toward Nauiyu in the form of a plan to relocate the town to higher ground.
Labor MLA Dheran Young, who represents the Daly electorate in the Territory parliament, said it was disappointing the community had been left behind
"The CLP government need to apply for the Commonwealth Disaster Relief Fund to ensure services can get back up and running," he said.
"To date, my understanding is that they haven't applied after the disaster relief fund under these extraordinary circumstances."
In August, the Commonwealth made a million-dollar investment in Nauiyu through the National Indigenous Australians Agency.
"The scale of damage experienced by the community has been immense," Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said.
"These investments will support community-led recovery efforts, helping to restore critical community facilities [and] strengthen local services."
The funding package, primarily aimed at local Indigenous corporations, sought to restore essential services, assets and accommodation for key workers.
The Northern Territory government did not respond to questions on Nauiyu or the recovery.
Mr Parry said the community has been visited by engineers and other personnel planning the town's relocation, in accordance with the NT government's investment.
He was frustrated, however, that there has not been more action ahead of the coming wet season.
"You got mango flowering now, you got tamarind, you got the cashew; those three things tell you that the rain's on the way here," he said.
With the near future uncertain, he wants a solid commitment from governments that funding will flow through to key services, and a plan will be in place should flooding re-occur.
"They've got everything, they've got homes to go to," he said.
"We lost everything, we started from scratch."
